parts.label: Part 4
parts.article:
Part four. You will hear an anthropology lecturer talking about early migration to the Americas. First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty on page six.

Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

Scientists from several different disciplines, anthropology, archaeology, and geology all agree that at some stage there was human migration from Asia to the Americas, but they disagree over when, how, or why these humans first came to the Americas.

I'll run through some of the evidence briefly and try to explain the timeframe, method, and reason for these migrations.

For a long time, most scientists had accepted that the original route into the Americas was from Northern Asia to Alaska. In the far North America, evidence suggests that humans arrived via a land bridge. This consisted of a dry grassland plain about two thousand kilometers wide. They think this environment would have been similar to present-day tundra with long, cool winters and perpetual winds, but crucially, no ice.

Geologists estimate that the land bridge existed between seventy-five thousand and fourteen thousand years ago. The theory is that these first humans were hunting animals, which they followed into what is now Alaska. Biological evidence as well as archaeological remains have been found which support this theory. For example, anthropologists have found a high incidence of similarly shaped teeth in people in Northern Asia and in North America.

The archaeological evidence also indicates that from Alaska in North America, people began to travel far south.

The problem is no one's sure yet what route people took or how humans would have been able to survive because much of the land would have still been covered in glaciers and it would have been very hard to find resources.

The other problem with this theory was that the evidence from Alaska only dated back thirteen thousand years.

This was in the form of weapons used for hunting. But evidence found at human settlements in other parts of the Americas dated further back than this.

The most significant of these settlements is on Monte Verde site in Chile in South America.

Evidence from the site includes biological remains which date back over fourteen thousand years, making Monte Verde the earliest known human settlement in the Americas.

This meant the date of the arrival of humans in Alaska had to be revised backwards by about two thousand years.

Some scientists also think that the first settlers moved down in haste from North to South America on the Pacific side, and findings at Monte Verde would seem to support this view.

Although no boats have been discovered yet to support this theory, we all know that earlier people in other parts of the world had made use of this technology.

The site at Monte Verde was discovered in nineteen seventy-six, and excavations revealed a small settlement of twenty to thirty people living in a dozen huts along a small stream. Scientists were surprised to discover nine species of marine plants, including seaweed material that the Monte Verdeans must have brought from the sea, which is over sixty kilometers away.

A variety of other items, including flat pebbles, were also found, which suggests the group had a tradition of exploring the sea.

However, there are still a number of prominent archaeologists who don't accept that the first humans arrived via Alaska and have put forward a theory of transoceanic migration instead.

They say that at this time, the climate in Alaska would have been too inhospitable for humans to survive in, and so the first people must have arrived across the Pacific Ocean.

Again, there's a lot of controversy surrounding this theory.

Many scientists doubt that people at this time had the navigational expertise for such a long voyage.

However, this idea does offer an alternative explanation as to how people were able to settle as far south as Monte Verde.

People who support this theory believe that crossing the Pacific would have been possible because of a powerful current in the Pacific Ocean, which would have carried boats from Japan to America.

Again, there's no real evidence to support this theory, but some archaeologists believe.

That is the end of part four. You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.

analyses.content: 听到录音中“long, cool winters and perpetual winds”对应题干的寒冷漫长和强风后，紧接着的“no ice”就对应了题目的“free from”，所以填ice。
They think this environment would've been similar to present-day tundra with long, cool winters and perpetual winds, but crucially, no ice.
你可能会因为没反应过来“no”和“free from”的同义替换，导致漏掉答案。
The theory is that these first humans were hunting animals, which they followed into what is now Alaska.
你可能会因为听到“hunting”就急着把它填进去，但要注意横线前是“followed”，跟在后面的是动物本身而不是打猎动作。
录音提到最早的人类在打猎，并且“followed”（跟随）这些“animals”进入了现在的阿拉斯加。
For example, anthropologists have found a high incidence of similarly shaped teeth in people in Northern Asia and in North America.
题目信息重合度极高，你只要稍微走神就容易错过“similarly shaped”这个提示词，从而导致漏听答案。
录音中“similarly shaped”几乎原词重现，后面紧跟的名词“teeth”就是正确答案。

The problem is no one's sure yet what route people took or how humans would've been able to survive because much of the land would've still been covered in glaciers and it would've been very hard to find resources.
这句话前面铺垫很长，你可能会在听到glaciers之后失去耐心，没有一直听到句末真正的考点。
录音提到被“glaciers”（冰川）覆盖，导致“very hard to find”（同义替换题干的difficult to find），后面跟着的就是答案resources。

The other problem with this theory was that the evidence from Alaska only dated back thirteen thousand years. This was in the form of weapons used for hunting, but evidence found at human settlements in other parts of the Americas dated further back than this.
你可能会因为上一句的“evidence”没有听清，导致没跟上这句“in the form of”的关键结构。
录音明确说到证据的形式是“in the form of weapons”，并且用途是“for hunting”，完全对应题干。
录音用“Although no boats have been discovered”表达了没有发现船只来支持这个理论，“discovered”替换了题目的“found”。
Although no boats have been discovered yet to support this theory, we all know that earlier people in other parts of the world had made use of this technology.
录音一开头就直接引出否定，你可能会期待先听到“support the theory”再找答案，从而错过了放在最前面的考点。
Scientists were surprised to discover nine species of marine plants, including seaweed material that the Monte Verdeans must have brought from the sea, which is over sixty kilometers away.
你可能会把“species”或者“marine”误当成答案，但题目要求填一个词且前面限制了“in the sea”（对应marine），所以只能填核心名词plants。
录音提到发现了九种海洋“plants”，并且用“including seaweed”举例，完全对应题干的“such as seaweed”。
They say that at this time, the climate in Alaska would've been too inhospitable for humans to survive in, and so the first people must have arrived across the Pacific Ocean.
你可能会听不懂“inhospitable”（不适宜居住的）这个生词，导致不敢确认它前面的climate就是你要找的答案。
录音中用“too inhospitable”替换了题干的“too bad”，而描述的对象正是主语“climate”。
Many scientists doubt that people at this time had the navigational expertise for such a long voyage.
你可能会因为“navigational”发音较长且是形容词，平时背得不够熟练，导致拼写错误或听到后没反应过来。
录音直接说到科学家怀疑当时人们的“navigational expertise”（航海技能），用“expertise”替换了题干的“skills”。
People who support this theory believe that crossing the Pacific would've been possible because of a powerful current in the Pacific Ocean, which would've carried boats from Japan to America.
你可能会因为一直死等“Pacific Ocean”这个词出现，反而忽略了它前面的修饰词powerful带出的核心答案。
录音用“powerful”替换了题干的“strong”，后面紧接的名词“current”（洋流）就是正确答案。
